Skoda Yeti goes for an off-roading feel
In the boot, the cube shape is emphasized by the distinct tribal patterns on the carpet, and it offers various small storage options along with room for a wheelchair in two of the full-size, separate seats.
Skoda appears to have opted for buttons and dials instead of the latest technology for the Yeti. This will likely suit many buyers, although personal music players and Blackberrys may not be capable of being used via Bluetooth or through a plug socket.
There is ample passenger ergonomics - you’re likely to find little to fault with the Yeti’s interior, especially regarding the B&O sound system that offers high-quality bass notes and rich mid-range sound.
One aspect of the Yeti that does not easily shed is its loudly rumbling ride. A soft, damp ride coupled with a loud, high-pitched roar at high speeds can be tiresome quickly; however, for city driving, the experience is quite different.
Add to that a high centre of gravity in the optional four-wheel drive models, and you end up with suppressed sportiness off-road.
You might not often find yourself critically exposed to roofing or rock climbing with a Yeti, and the extra unladen weight accounts for much of its 640kg mass, making it a straightforward yet mildly noisy travel companion.
You will notice the hallmarks of German engineering, which are highlighted in the well-judged four-wheel drive models.
There is ample relaxed work available with the Yeti, but the dynamic models present a somewhat perverse and awkward car that requires significant coaxing to achieve secure, predictable, and safe handling.
